questions.solution:
For mirrors: $\mathbf{\dfrac{1}{v} + \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f}}$.

For lenses the sign is different: $\dfrac1v - \dfrac1u = \dfrac1f$. Mixing the two up is the most common error in this chapter — mirrors add, lenses subtract.

questions.q: Total internal reflection can occur only when light travels:
questions.solution:
It needs the ray to bend **away** from the normal, which happens only going from **denser to rarer** — and only beyond the critical angle.

$\sin C = \dfrac{1}{\mu}$ (rarer medium being air). It is what keeps light inside an optical fibre and what makes a diamond sparkle.

questions.q: The power of a lens of focal length $50$ cm is:
questions.solution:
$P = \dfrac{1}{f\text{ (in metres)}} = \dfrac{1}{0.5} = \mathbf{2}$ D.

The focal length must be in **metres** — the single most common slip here.

questions.q: Light travels from air into a medium of refractive index $1.5$. Its speed in the medium is:
questions.solution:
$\mu = \dfrac{c}{v} \Rightarrow v = \dfrac{3 \times 10^{8}}{1.5} = \mathbf{2 \times 10^{8}}$ m/s.

The frequency does not change when light enters a new medium — the wavelength does, and with it the speed.

questions.q: In a compound microscope, the objective forms an image that is:
questions.solution:
The object sits just beyond the objective's focus, so the objective forms a **real, inverted, magnified** image inside the tube.

The eyepiece then acts as a simple magnifier on that image, giving a final image that is virtual, further magnified, and still inverted with respect to the object.

questions.q: An object is placed $30$ cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length $20$ cm. Find the image distance, in cm (give the magnitude).
questions.solution:
Using magnitudes with the real-is-positive convention: $\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{f} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{20} - \dfrac{1}{30} = \dfrac{3 - 2}{60} = \dfrac{1}{60}$.

$v = \mathbf{60}$ cm — a real, inverted image, magnified twice, formed on the same side as the object.

questions.q: An object is $20$ cm from a convex lens of focal length $10$ cm. Find the image distance, in cm (give the magnitude).
questions.solution:
Working in magnitudes for a real object and a converging lens, $\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{f} - \dfrac{1}{u}$:

$\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{10} - \dfrac{1}{20} = \dfrac{1}{20}$, so $v = \mathbf{20}$ cm.

An object at $2f$ gives an image at $2f$, the same size and inverted — the one case worth remembering without calculation.

questions.q: Find the critical angle (in degrees) for a medium of refractive index $2$ in contact with air.
questions.solution:
$\sin C = \dfrac{1}{\mu} = \dfrac12 \Rightarrow C = \mathbf{30°}$.

The higher the refractive index, the smaller the critical angle — which is why diamond ($\mu = 2.42$, $C \approx 24°$) traps light so well.

questions.q: Two thin lenses of powers $+3$ D and $-1$ D are placed in contact. Find the power of the combination, in dioptres.
questions.solution:
Powers in contact simply add: $3 + (-1) = \mathbf{2}$ D.

The combination has focal length $\dfrac{1}{2} = 0.5$ m, and it is converging.

questions.q: An object $4$ cm tall gives an image $12$ cm tall. Find the magnitude of the magnification.
questions.solution:
$|m| = \dfrac{h_{i}}{h_{o}} = \dfrac{12}{4} = \mathbf{3}$.

A negative $m$ would mean the image is inverted; a magnitude greater than 1 means enlarged.

questions.q: State the lens maker's formula and use it to find the focal length of a biconvex lens of refractive index $1.5$ with both radii $20$ cm.
questions.solution:
$\dfrac{1}{f} = \left(\mu - 1\right)\left(\dfrac{1}{R_{1}} - \dfrac{1}{R_{2}}\right)$.

For a biconvex lens, $R_{1} = +20$ cm and $R_{2} = -20$ cm (the second surface curves the other way).

$\dfrac1f = (1.5 - 1)\left(\dfrac{1}{20} - \dfrac{1}{-20}\right) = 0.5 \times \dfrac{2}{20} = \dfrac{1}{20}$.

$f = \mathbf{20}$ cm, converging.

The formula also explains why a lens behaves differently in water: $\mu$ is the refractive index **relative to the surrounding medium**, so a glass lens in water is much weaker, and a lens of lower index than its surroundings changes from converging to diverging.

questions.q: Derive the relation between the angle of prism $A$, the angle of minimum deviation $\delta_{m}$ and the refractive index $\mu$.
questions.solution:
At minimum deviation the ray passes **symmetrically**: the angles of incidence and emergence are equal ($i = e$), and so are the two refraction angles ($r_{1} = r_{2} = r$).

**From the prism geometry:** $A = r_{1} + r_{2} = 2r$, so $r = \dfrac{A}{2}$.

**From the deviation:** $\delta = i + e - A$, so at minimum $\delta_{m} = 2i - A$, giving $i = \dfrac{A + \delta_{m}}{2}$.

**Snell's law at the first face:**

$\mu = \dfrac{\sin i}{\sin r} = \mathbf{\dfrac{\sin\left(\dfrac{A + \delta_{m}}{2}\right)}{\sin\left(\dfrac{A}{2}\right)}}$.

The symmetry at minimum deviation is not an accident: the path is reversible, and the deviation curve is flat at its lowest point, so the symmetric path is the one that achieves it.

questions.q: Draw in words the ray diagram of a compound microscope and derive its magnifying power when the final image is at the near point.
questions.solution:
**Arrangement.** The objective has a short focal length $f_{o}$; the object is placed just beyond $f_{o}$, so a real, inverted, magnified image forms inside the tube. That image falls just inside the eyepiece's focus, and the eyepiece magnifies it further into a virtual image at the near point.

**Objective's magnification:** $m_{o} = \dfrac{v_{o}}{u_{o}}$, which for a tube of length $L$ is approximately $\dfrac{L}{f_{o}}$.

**Eyepiece's magnification** (image at near point $D$): $m_{e} = 1 + \dfrac{D}{f_{e}}$.

**Total:**

$\mathbf{m = \dfrac{L}{f_{o}}\left(1 + \dfrac{D}{f_{e}}\right)}$.

So both focal lengths must be **short** — which is exactly how a microscope is built, and why the objective sits so close to the slide.

With the image at infinity instead (relaxed eye), $m_{e} = \dfrac{D}{f_{e}}$ and the total is a little smaller but more comfortable to look through for long.

questions.q: State the conditions for total internal reflection and explain how an optical fibre uses it.
questions.solution:
**Conditions.**

1. Light must travel from a **denser** medium to a **rarer** one.

2. The angle of incidence must exceed the **critical angle** $C$, where $\sin C = \dfrac{\mu_{\text{rarer}}}{\mu_{\text{denser}}}$.

**In an optical fibre.** A core of high refractive index is surrounded by cladding of lower index. Light entering at a shallow enough angle strikes the core–cladding boundary beyond the critical angle and is **totally** reflected — no refracted ray escapes and, unlike a mirror, nothing is absorbed.

It bounces along the fibre this way for kilometres, following its bends, with very little loss.

'Total' is the operative word: an ordinary mirror loses a few per cent at every bounce, and over thousands of reflections that would leave nothing.

questions.q: An object is placed $15$ cm in front of a convex lens of focal length $10$ cm. Find the position and nature of the image.
questions.solution:
Using the Cartesian convention with $u = -15$ cm and $f = +10$ cm:

$\dfrac1v - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac1f \Rightarrow \dfrac1v = \dfrac{1}{10} + \dfrac{1}{-15} = \dfrac{3 - 2}{30} = \dfrac{1}{30}$.

$v = \mathbf{+30}$ cm — positive, so the image is **real** and on the far side of the lens.

**Magnification:** $m = \dfrac{v}{u} = \dfrac{30}{-15} = -2$, so the image is **inverted and twice the size**.

The object lies between $f$ and $2f$, and that always gives a real, inverted, magnified image beyond $2f$ — which is exactly how a projector is set up.
